client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I can't seem to focus on my university work at all — I'll sit down to read or write something and my mind just goes blank, or I end up crying instead. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, but I didn't know what else to do.
therapist:
It takes real courage to reach out even when you're not sure it will help, and I'm truly glad you did. Losing your grandmother and then trying to carry on with university work is an enormous weight to bear — the way your mind goes blank or tears come instead of words makes complete sense, because grief has its own timeline that doesn't pause for deadlines. 

I'm wondering, when you sit down to study and that wave of emotion comes over you, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind in those moments?

client: Honestly, the main thing I keep thinking is that I should be over this by now, or at least functional enough to get my work done. Like there's this voice in my head saying my grandmother wouldn't want me to fall behind, that she'd be disappointed in me for letting everything slip. And then I feel guilty on top of everything else, which just makes it harder to concentrate.
therapist:
That thought — that you *should* be over this by now — is such a common but really painful one to carry, and it's worth gently noticing that you're grieving someone you clearly loved deeply, just one month ago, which is no time at all. It's also interesting that the voice invoking your grandmother is framing her as disappointed, when it sounds like she was someone important enough to you that her loss has shaken your whole world — I wonder if that's really her voice, or a harsher critic that's borrowed her name. 

What do you think your grandmother was actually like — the real her — when you were struggling with something difficult in the past?

client: That's... actually a hard question to sit with, because when I really think about her, she was never harsh with me. When I was struggling with my exams in high school she just made me tea and sat with me, she didn't lecture me or make me feel like I was failing. But I don't know, even knowing that, it doesn't quite turn off that critical voice — it's like I understand it logically but I can't feel it, if that makes sense.
therapist:
What you just described — knowing something logically but not being able to *feel* it — is one of the most honest and common experiences in grief, and it makes complete sense that your heart hasn't caught up with your head yet. The fact that you could recall her so vividly just now, making tea and simply *being with you* in your struggle, tells me that somewhere inside you already know what she'd actually offer you right now — and it isn't disappointment. 

I'm curious: if you tried to treat yourself this week even a little the way she treated you during those high school exams, what might that look like for you?

client: I guess it might look like... giving myself permission to take breaks without feeling like I'm being lazy, or maybe making myself a cup of tea when I sit down to study instead of just forcing my way through it. But honestly, it feels a bit silly, like I'm just looking for excuses not to work when I already have so much to catch up on. I'm worried that if I'm too gentle with myself I'll just completely fall apart and never get anything done.
therapist:
That fear — that self-compassion is a slippery slope to falling apart completely — is so understandable, but it's worth noticing that the harsh, pushing approach hasn't been getting you to your work either, so it might not be protecting you in the way you hope. The tea, the permission to breathe — that's not an excuse, that's actually what your grandmother instinctively knew you needed to *function*, not just to feel better. 

What if we thought of it as a small experiment rather than a permanent change — just trying her way for a day or two and seeing what actually happens to your ability to work?

client: I suppose framing it as an experiment makes it feel slightly less scary, like I'm not committing to something that might make everything worse. But I'm still worried about the practical side — I have an essay due in two weeks and I'm so far behind that even a day or two of being gentle with myself feels like a luxury I can't afford right now. I guess I just don't know how to balance actually grieving with still being a student.
therapist:
That tension you're naming — between being a grieving person and a functioning student — is so real, and I want to gently offer that these might not be as opposed as they feel right now; sometimes allowing yourself small moments of grief actually frees up the mental space that's currently being consumed by fighting it. It might also be worth considering whether your university has any support in place — extensions or counselling — because reaching out there wouldn't be giving up, it would be the practical, wise thing to do given what you're carrying.

For the essay itself, I'm wondering what the very smallest possible step might look like — not catching up, just one tiny thing — that might feel manageable alongside a cup of tea this week?

client: Maybe the smallest step would be just opening the essay document and reading what I've already written, without any pressure to add anything new. I've actually thought about asking for an extension before, but I feel embarrassed about it — like I'd have to explain everything to my professor and I don't really want to talk about my grandmother with someone I barely know. It feels exposing in a way that I'm not sure I'm ready for.
therapist:
Opening the document and simply reading — no pressure to add a single word — sounds like exactly the right-sized step, and I want you to notice that you came up with that yourself, which matters. On the extension, most universities actually allow you to request support through a pastoral or wellbeing office rather than directly to your professor, which means you might not have to explain your grandmother to anyone you don't feel safe with — just a brief note that you're dealing with a bereavement can often be enough. 

How would it feel to look into that pathway this week, so you at least know what your options are without having to commit to anything yet?

client: That actually sounds more manageable than I'd imagined — I think I assumed it would have to be this big, formal conversation and knowing it might just be a brief note makes it feel less overwhelming. I think I could probably look into it, though I'd likely spend a while just staring at the webpage without actually doing anything. I'm a bit like that when I'm anxious — I research things to death instead of actually taking the step.
therapist:
It's really self-aware of you to notice that pattern — researching as a way of feeling like you're doing something while also staying safely on the edge of actually doing it, which is such a human response to anxiety. I wonder if we could apply the same logic as the essay: maybe the smallest step isn't filling out any forms, but just finding the webpage and saving the link, so that future-you doesn't have to search for it when she's ready to take the next step.

What do you think would make it more likely that you'd actually open that page rather than putting it off — is there a time or a small ritual, like that cup of tea, that might help?

client: Maybe I could try doing it tomorrow morning before I've had time to talk myself out of it, with a cup of tea like you said — there's something about mornings where I haven't yet built up all the reasons not to do something. But I'm a little worried that even that small step will make everything feel more real, like once I officially tell the university I'm grieving it becomes this formal thing and I can't just pretend I'm coping anymore. I think part of me has been holding on to that pretense because letting go of it feels like admitting how much I'm actually struggling.
therapist:
What you just said is really profound — that the pretense of coping has been a way of protecting yourself from the full weight of how hard this actually is, and that makes complete sense as something to hold onto. But I want to gently reflect back that you've already let go of that pretense a little today, just by being here and saying out loud how much you're struggling — and you haven't fallen apart, you've actually found some clarity and a plan. 

I'm wondering if admitting you're grieving to the university might feel less like losing control, and more like finally giving yourself the same honest acknowledgment you've already been brave enough to give yourself in this conversation today?

client: I hadn't thought about it that way, that I've already kind of done the scary thing just by being here today. That actually does reframe it a little, though I'm not sure one conversation is quite the same as having it on record somewhere official. But maybe you're right that I've been treating the pretense like it's keeping me safe when really it's just keeping me isolated with all of this.
therapist:
That last thing you said — that the pretense has been keeping you isolated — feels like a really important insight, because grief is so much harder to carry alone, and every step you've taken today, reaching out, remembering who your grandmother really was, finding your own small steps, has been you gently loosening that isolation. You're right that one conversation isn't the same as an official record, but what strikes me is that you came in unsure talking would even help, and something has shifted a little. 

As you go into tomorrow morning with your tea and that webpage, I'm curious — is there anyone in your life, a friend or family member, who might be able to sit with you in that moment the way your grandmother once sat with you during your exams?

client: There's one friend from my course who I think would understand, but I've been pulling away from her lately because I don't want to be a burden or have to explain why I've been so absent. I think I've been telling myself she's probably frustrated with me for going quiet, but honestly I don't actually know that — I've just been assuming it. It's easier to stay distant than to find out whether I've damaged things by disappearing.
therapist:
You just caught yourself doing something really important — you noticed that you've been treating an assumption as if it were a fact, without any actual evidence that she's frustrated, which is exactly the kind of thought worth gently questioning. It's also worth noticing that this is the second time today you've imagined someone who cares about you — first your grandmother, now your friend — as harsher and more disappointed than they've actually shown themselves to be, which might say more about how hard you're being on yourself right now than about them. 

I wonder, if your friend had gone quiet for a month after losing someone she loved, what would you actually feel towards her — frustration, or something else entirely?
